name: Intransitive Preposition Use

dimensions.form: Preposition heading a PP without an NP object; it may be complementless or take a PP, clause, or predicative complement
dimensions.meaning: Varies with the head and complement: location, direction, time, reason, comparison, and other relations
dimensions.function: Heads an intransitive PP in complement, modifier, adjunct, or predicative function
dimensions.distribution: The full CGEL objectless class; complementless locative members occupy the same PP positions as full locative PPs

1.definition: A preposition used without an NP object, whether or not it has another kind of complement
1.details: Intransitive means no object, not no complement. A complementless member such as outside heads a one-word PP, but an intransitive preposition may instead take a PP complement (owing to the rain), a predicative complement (as satisfactory), or a clause complement (because it rained). Ago is intransitive-only and occurs with an obligatory pre-head measure modifier (ten years ago; cf. ten years before Christ). The category remains preposition throughout (CGEL p. 272); the analysis of ago deliberately rejects CGEL p. 632.

constraints.description: The head has no NP object in this use; the presence of a non-object complement does not make the PP transitive.
Within the complementless locative subset, right/straight modification and from-embedding help distinguish PPs from AdvPs (right outside, straight home, from abroad).

projection.target: Outside can occur alone in We waited outside or with a complement in We waited outside the gate. The ability to say from outside supplies a test beyond merely counting overt NP complements.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes intransitive uses and documents PP embedding by from and other prepositions.

curious.title: Prepositions with no object
curious.summary: Some prepositions can do their job without a noun phrase after them, as outside does in She waited outside.
curious.body:
Take in the garden: the preposition in has an object, the garden. But in She waited outside, outside stands alone. It has no object, yet it's still the same kind of word, a preposition.

No object doesn't mean nothing follows. A preposition can take a phrase, as in owing to the rain, a description, as in as satisfactory, or a whole clause, as in because it rained. What it lacks is a noun phrase object.
curious.try: Say We waited outside and We waited outside the gate. What does the gate add?

teacher.summary: Explains that prepositions can be intransitive, lacking an object, without lacking a complement.
teacher.explain: Intransitive here means no object, not no complement. A preposition without an NP object can be complementless, as in outside, or can take a PP complement (owing to the rain), a predicative complement (as satisfactory), or a clause complement (because it rained). The category remains preposition throughout. The PP can function as complement, modifier, adjunct or predicative. For complementless locative members such as outside, right or straight modification and from-embedding help distinguish PPs from adverb phrases: right outside, straight home, from abroad. This dictionary gives ago as intransitive-only, with an obligatory pre-head measure modifier, as in ten years ago. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: A word like outside in this use is sometimes called an adverb. CGEL, and this dictionary, treat them as prepositions heading PPs without an object.

contrasts.note: The same word with a noun phrase object.

watch_for: A learner might think a preposition must be followed by a noun phrase.
A learner might read no object as meaning no complement, when to the rain (after owing) and it rained (after because) are complements.
teacher.activity: Students list prepositions from a text and sort each use by whether a noun phrase object follows. They then find uses with a PP, predicative or clause complement.
